transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-20
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Horizon CISO), Mark Patel (Head Infra), Sofia Ruiz (Security Engineer)

Auto-generated Summary: Encryption-focused security review; BYOK/HSM questions, SOC2 and audit logs discussed.

00:00 Speaker 1 (Jordan): hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick intro — i'm jordan, ae at redwood. priya is our se, she'll run through the tech details.
00:18 Speaker 2 (Priya): hi all, thanks. i'll start with a quick overview of how we handle encryption at rest and in transit, and then we can dive into BYOK/HSM details. feel free to interrupt.
00:34 Speaker 3 (Lena): sounds good. just to set context, we're evaluating for customer-facing payment flows. regulatory constraints mean we need control over keys; we also have strict data residency in eu and us-east.
00:50 Speaker 1 (Jordan): got it. timeline? you're aiming for pilot q3?  
01:02 Speaker 3 (Lena): yes, pilot in september, prod late q4. compliance gating from our side — SOC 2 type II and iso 27001 evidence.
01:20 Speaker 2 (Priya): perfect. so first, encryption in transit: we use tls 1.2/1.3 for all service-to-service and client communications, mTLS optional for private deployments. for hosted api we terminate tls at redwood edge and it's encrypted on the wire to our control plane, and we also support dedicated/private paths where customers can enforce mTLS to their endpoints.
01:45 Speaker 3 (Lena): when you say terminate at edge, do we have options for customer-managed certs? we need that for some auditors.
01:55 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, for private deployments you can bring your own certs; for hosted we can support customer-managed certs via our enterprise proxy or mutual tls layers — i'll follow up with exact config examples.
02:10 Speaker 4 (Mark): moving to at-rest — what's your default encryption and where do keys live?
02:18 Speaker 2 (Priya): at-rest data is encrypted using AES-256. by default we manage the KMS keys in the cloud provider (for hosted). customers can opt for CMEK/bring-your-own-key (BYOK). we support cloud KMS integrations and also an HSM-backed BYOK flow where the customer's key material never leaves their HSM.
02:45 Speaker 4 (Mark): ok, so for BYOK, do you support importable keys or do you do a wrapped key model? what's the envelope flow?
02:55 Speaker 2 (Priya): good question. we use an envelope encryption model. the data encryption keys are generated per-tenant and wrapped with a customer-managed key in their KMS/HSM. for cloud kms we create a CMEK binding; for on-prem/customer-hsm we accept wrapped keys and do a zero-knowledge handshake so we never see raw key material. 
03:20 Speaker 3 (Lena): can you walk through the zero-knowledge handshake a bit more? auditors will ask.
03:28 Speaker 2 (Priya): sure — during onboarding we generate a random DEK locally in our runtime, then we use the customer's public wrapping key (or kms api) to wrap that dek. the wrapped dek is stored with the tenant metadata. decryption requires an unwrap call against the customer's kms/hsm. in private deployments the unwrap can happen inside the customer's vpc/on-prem so keys don't cross network boundaries. there's also support for hsm signed attestations to prove key provenance.
03:55 Speaker 1 (Jordan): just to add — we can provide a technical runbook that shows the exact api calls and sample configs for aws kms, gcp kms, azure key vault, and common hsm vendors.
04:08 Speaker 4 (Mark): what about key rotation and rotation windows? we have strict rotation policies.
04:16 Speaker 2 (Priya): we support scheduled rotation of customer master keys (CMK) and DEKs. rotations can be orchestrated via the customer's KMS or via our orchestration layer, but for BYOK the rotation lifecycle is controlled by the customer. we also maintain key version metadata and can rewrap DEKs with a new CMK when rotation occurs. note: rewrapping is a metadata operation unless you opt to re-encrypt historical blobs.
04:40 Speaker 3 (Lena): do you maintain audit logs for all unwrap/cryptographic operations?
04:46 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, all unwrap/wrap operations generate audit entries. for hosted, logs are sent to our secure logging pipeline and can be exported via secure s3/gcs/az blob or pushed to the customer's SIEM via syslog/secure forwarder. we keep detailed logs: timestamp, operation, key id, requester id, request origin ip (where available).
05:10 Speaker 4 (Mark): retention of those logs — can we define retention and access controls? some of our logs require 7-year retention for certain jurisdictions.
05:20 Speaker 2 (Priya): we have configurable retention windows and support long-term archival to customer buckets. access is RBAC controlled; we can integrate with your SSO/SAML to map roles. for ultra-sensitive logs you can opt to retain only in your storage and we won't copy.
05:36 Speaker 3 (Lena): on SSO and RBAC — how granular is your RBAC? can we restrict key unwrap to a service account only?
05:44 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, our RBAC supports role-based policies down to the service-level. you can require that unwrap calls only come from a specific service principal or machine identity. we integrate with OIDC/SAML and can map groups to roles. in dedicated/private installs you have full control of authN and can disable our control plane auth paths.
06:05 Speaker 4 (Mark): auditors will ask for separation of duties and proof of key custody. do you offer attestation docs or hsm logs?
06:15 Speaker 2 (Priya): we provide attestation packages and HSM integration notes. for HSM-backed BYOK, we can collect HSM audit logs or provide pointers to the vendor attestation. we also provide a signed certificate of key generation event (depending on the HSM vendor capabilities).
06:35 Speaker 1 (Jordan): quick q from sales side — any specific vendors you're using for HSM or cloud?  
06:42 Speaker 4 (Mark): we run thales and aws cloudhsm for some workloads. we also use aws kms for non-hsm keys.
06:50 Speaker 2 (Priya): we have prior integrations with aws kms, gcp kms, azure key vault, thales nshield and other hsm providers via standard pkcs#11 and cloudhsm apis. for thales we support wrapping via a customer-supplied public key and for cloudhsm we can do an unwrap API call that stays inside the vpc.
07:10 Speaker 3 (Lena): network flows — during unwrap, does anything traverse the public internet for hosted option? our network team will want to know.
07:20 Speaker 2 (Priya): for hosted with customer-managed kms in a cloud provider, we call the kms endpoints over the internet (tls) but we recommend using a private endpoint or vpc peering for low risk. for dedicated/private we always encourage a private link so unwraps occur inside the provider network. we can also support a proxy that routes kms calls back to your on-prem HSM via secure tunnel.
07:45 Speaker 4 (Mark): any performance implications for unwrap on every request? token throughput matters for us.
07:52 Speaker 2 (Priya): unwrap is relatively expensive; our runtime caches unwrapped DEKs in memory (kv cache) for a configurable TTL. unwrap calls are only needed when cache expires or on key rotation. we can tune TTL to your security policies; we also support ephemeral DEKs per session to reduce exposure.
08:15 Speaker 3 (Lena): we want to ensure if a key is revoked, no decrypts happen afterwards. how fast is revocation enforced?
08:24 Speaker 2 (Priya): revocation is immediate. once a CMK is disabled or marked revoked in your KMS/HSM, unwrap calls will fail. our cache respects key usability metadata and will purge DEKs if the backing CMK is revoked — typically within seconds to minutes depending on TTL.
08:46 Speaker 4 (Mark): ok. on data residency — can you pin storage and inference to eu-only zones?
08:53 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, for private/dedicated we can pin deployments to regions and storage to region-specific buckets. for hosted we have regions and can route requests and storage to a specified region; we can also do geofencing policies on request routing.
09:14 Speaker 3 (Lena): auditors want separation between logs and keys — any co-location concerns?
09:21 Speaker 2 (Priya): we keep key metadata separate from application logs; wrapped DEKs and key metadata are stored in a secure keystore with restricted access. logs can be exported to your buckets; we won't store plaintext data and it's separated in different storage classes and accounts.
09:40 Speaker 4 (Mark): what about HSM attestation proof for key origin? our compliance team wants CA-signed attestation.
09:48 Speaker 2 (Priya): depends on the HSM vendor; we can provide vendor-signed attestations or signed key creation events (for example, nshield has modules for signed attestations). we'll document the exact artifacts per vendor.
10:05 Speaker 3 (Lena): can you provide sample audit logs for unwrap operations? need to show typical fields.
10:12 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, we'll share a sanitized sample log with fields: timestamp, operation, key_id, wrapped_dek_id, requestor_id, requester_ip, outcome, correlation_id. sample attached in follow-up.
10:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): quick pricing flag — HSM-backed BYOK often impacts cost; we can include a dedicated lane estimate. we'll follow up with numbers.
10:40 Speaker 3 (Lena): another question — are you SOC2 certified and do you have iso 27001? and can we get the reports under NDA?
10:48 Speaker 1 (Jordan): we are SOC 2 Type II; iso 27001 cert in our security pack. we can share reports under nda — i'll attach them in the follow-up.
11:00 Speaker 4 (Mark): ok. on the technical side — for private deployment, can we host the control plane inside our vpc so that unwraps never leave the vpc?
11:10 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, our private deployment option gives you a private control plane; unwraps and key material handling can all stay inside your network. for some customers we run a hybrid where control plane is customer-managed and Redwood provides the runtime.
11:30 Speaker 3 (Lena): do you support hardware attestation for runtime nodes? we use it for supply chain.
11:36 Speaker 2 (Priya): we support intel sgx attestation options and also signed node enrollment via vault-like PKI in private deployments.
11:50 Speaker 4 (Mark): if we have a regulator asking for chain of custody for keys over the last year, do you have historical key events?
11:58 Speaker 2 (Priya): yes, we keep key event history (creation, rotation, revoke, access attempts) as part of the audit trail. these can be exported.
12:15 Speaker 3 (Lena): about breach notification — what's your expected SLA on notifying customers if we suspect key compromise?
12:24 Speaker 1 (Jordan): we have incident response playbooks and contractual notification timelines. for keys specifically, we'd notify immediately and coordinate remediation with your security team per the SLA — we'll include specifics in our security docs.
12:40 Speaker 4 (Mark): one last detail — do you support multi-region keys or key replication for DR?
12:47 Speaker 2 (Priya): we support multi-region key strategies. for BYOK, replication is handled by your KMS; for our managed keys we can replicate wrapped DEKs across regions using cross-region replication patterns while preserving envelope protection.
13:05 Speaker 3 (Lena): great, any blocker on us running a POC with HSM-backed BYOK in a staging env?
13:12 Speaker 2 (Priya): no blocker; we recommend a scoped poc: we'll set up a staging project with CMEK enabled, a test hsm connector, and run throughput tests to validate unwrap latency and caching. Priya will run the tech onboarding and Mark's team can provide the HSM endpoint.
13:30 Speaker 1 (Jordan): recap before we go: action items — we'll send SOC2/ISO, priya will share the KMS runbook and hsm integration notes, we'll schedule the infra deep-dive and pricing. mark, lena, sofia will confirm availability for the week of 7/27.
13:50 Speaker 3 (Lena): sounds good. thanks.

30:10 Speaker 2 (Priya): older models may not support some automation APIs; we can do a manual onboarding flow or use wrapping via a provided public key. we'll detail per vendor.
36:00 Speaker 3 (Lena): okay that's useful. we'll review the runbook when you send it. thanks again.
